content: Sewage primarily consists of liquid waste generated by human activities, which includes washing water, feces, urine, laundry waste, and other materials that are disposed of through household and industrial drains and toilets. It is classified as a type of wastewater. Sewage management involves the collection, treatment, and either recycling or safe disposal of this waste into the environment. In the United States, as of 2004, approximately 850 billion gallons of untreated sewage were being discharged into waterways annually. Historically, large-scale sewage disposal systems were first designed by the architects of the Indus Valley Civilization. These systems included networks of brick-lined effluent drains that followed the layout of streets. The drains were constructed to be seven to ten feet wide and were positioned two feet below ground level, with U-shaped bottoms lined with loose bricks that could be easily removed for cleaning. At the intersections of these drains, cesspools were installed, complete with steps for access to facilitate periodic cleaning. By 2700 BCE, cities in this region had developed standardized earthenware plumbing pipes with broad flanges, which were joined using asphalt to prevent leaks. The earliest known sanitation systems were discovered in the prehistoric Middle East and surrounding areas. The first use of an inverted siphon system, along with glass-covered clay pipes, was documented in the palaces of Crete, Greece. Remarkably, this system remains functional after approximately 3,000 years. However, little progress was made in sewage systems until the 16th century. During this period, Sir John Harington in England invented a device for Queen Elizabeth I, his godmother, which directed waste into cesspools. Sewage collection and disposal are facilitated by a network of sewer pipes, collectively referred to as a sewerage system in British English or a sewage system in American English. These systems transport sewage to treatment facilities or designated disposal sites. In areas without access to a centralized sewerage system, sewage may be collected from homes via pipes leading to septic tanks or cesspits. Alternatively, it may be transported by vehicles to treatment facilities. Septic tanks, when functioning properly, require periodic emptying every two to five years, depending on the system's load. Sewage treatment involves the removal of contaminants from sewage to produce liquid and solid byproducts (sludge) that are safe for environmental discharge or reuse. This process is a critical component of waste management. On-site wastewater treatment systems, such as septic tanks or biofilters, can be employed to treat sewage near its source. Sewage water is a chemically complex mixture, characterized by high concentrations of ammonium, nitrate, and phosphorus, as well as elevated conductivity due to dissolved solids. It also exhibits high alkalinity, with a typical pH range of 7 to 8. Additionally, trihalomethanes may be present as a byproduct of past disinfection processes. In developed nations, sewage collection and treatment are regulated by local, state, and federal standards. The term sewage is derived from Old French seuwiere, Anglo-Norman sewere, or Anglo-French assewer and essiver, which mean to drain or to channel overflow from a fish pond. These terms ultimately trace back to the Vulgar Latin exaquare or exaquria, from Latin ex(out of) and aqua (water). Historically, the terms sewerage and sewage were used interchangeably, though this usage was incorrect. In modern American English, the distinction between the two terms is properly observed.
